content:
I've noticed recently that Apple appears to have given up on Cinematic mode, and a video experiment perfectly captures my disappointment with this fact.

It's not because the feature itself is bad, but because it's so close to being good enough, yet falls just short of being truly practical—it's hard to understand why Apple hasn't taken advantage of the massive performance leap from the iPhone 13 (the first phone to introduce this feature) to the latest iPhone. Let me show you…

I've said before that I understand why Apple hasn't made updating it a priority, but I also maintain that Apple should update it to encourage the next generation of video creators and filmmakers, especially teenagers who may not have access to other camera equipment.

I have a friend who frequently uses a smartphone to interview strangers on the street and always manages to get them to open up and share stories you could never imagine. I decided to reverse the roles and put him on a stool, filming him with a smartphone—this time, my iPhone 16 Pro Max.

I wanted to test how Cinematic mode would handle a relatively simple challenge: a person in the foreground, with railings about 25 feet behind him, and the O2 Arena on the other side of the Thames perhaps nearly a thousand feet away. Additionally, he'd be sitting on a stool, so his range of movement would be quite limited.

The answer is… just short of perfect. The overall effect is good, but there's noticeable haloing between CK's legs and the railings, the support pillars of the O2 sometimes lose focus when he moves his head, and when he spreads his hands wide, the river water occasionally comes into sharp focus:

To be fair, CK thinks the average viewer wouldn't notice these issues when watching the video. If they're not filmmakers or tech enthusiasts familiar with how this feature works, they might not even notice these flaws, and even if they do, they wouldn't find them bothersome. I reckon he makes a good point.

But these issues do bother me, and I believe even amateur film enthusiasts would share the same disappointment—and these people are precisely the target audience for this feature.

As I said at the beginning, my disappointment isn't because the feature is bad, but because I genuinely believe that if Apple could properly leverage the powerful performance and neural network processing capabilities of current iPhone chips, this feature could be significantly improved. In fact, I'd expect a properly updated Cinematic mode to be able to handle far more complex shooting environments than this.

Do you agree with my view? Do you want Apple to take Cinematic mode seriously? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.
